title: Gold Drops $100 in Sharpest Daily Fall as Oil Spike Fuels Rate-Hike Fears
excerpt: Precious metals sell off despite geopolitical turmoil as surging oil prices stoke inflation worries, but Citi and UBS see gold doubling in the long run.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Gold dropped 2.4% to $4,046.50, its largest fall since July 13.
  • Silver fell 3.7% to $57.80, marking its biggest decline in two weeks.
  • Citi predicts gold could drop 15-20% before potentially doubling past $6,000.
  • UBS targets gold at $4,675 by year-end, citing improving market sentiment.
  • Gold remains 23.9% below its all-time high of $5,318.40 from January.

Gold shed $100 an ounce on Thursday in its sharpest single-session decline in 10 days, falling 2.4% to $4,046.50 as an oil-price spike above $100 a barrel reignited inflation concerns and strengthened bets that central banks will keep interest rates elevated.

Silver fell even harder, losing 3.7% to close at $57.80 per ounce. The sell-off snapped gold’s two-session winning streak and pushed silver to its sixth-lowest settlement of 2026.

Oil Rally Drives Rate-Hike Fears

The catalyst was crude oil’s surge past $100 a barrel after Houthi forces attacked Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, compounding existing disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz. Rising energy costs feed directly into inflation expectations, making it harder for central banks to cut interest rates.

Higher rates diminish the appeal of non-yielding assets like gold. Investors now expect at least one rate hike by the Federal Reserve before year-end, with the central bank widely anticipated to hold rates unchanged at next week’s meeting.

“Rising oil prices amid escalating tensions in the Middle East have fueled concerns over global inflationary pressures and reinforced hawkish monetary policy expectations,” said Tony Sage of Critical Metals.

The Bull Case Remains Intact

Despite Thursday’s drop, several major banks remain bullish on gold’s medium-term trajectory. Citi Research’s Max Layton outlined a scenario in which gold falls another 15 to 20% from current levels — potentially testing the $3,400 range — before rebounding sharply past $6,000 per ounce.

“The longer-term outlook is very bullish, underpinned by numerous factors including China’s large trade surplus, China’s central bank buying, rising global fiscal sustainability issues, and high levels of global geopolitical tensions.”

— Max Layton, Citi Research

UBS strategist Joni Teves struck a similar tone, forecasting gold at $4,675 by year-end and $4,800 by the end of 2027. She noted sentiment toward gold was “starting to improve” after Hong Kong and China gold equities gained roughly 20% in three trading days.

By the Numbers

Gold remains 23.9% below its all-time high of $5,318.40, reached on January 29 this year, but sits 22.9% above its 52-week low of $3,293.20 from last July. Year-to-date, gold is down 6.5%, while silver has dropped 17.6%.

A packed calendar of central bank decisions looms. The European Central Bank announced its rate decision this week, with the Fed, Bank of Japan, and Bank of England all meeting next week. Each outcome carries implications for bond yields, currency markets, and gold’s near-term direction.

What It Means for Indian Investors

India is the world’s second-largest gold consumer, and price movements in New York and London directly affect rates in Mumbai and Delhi. Thursday’s decline translates to a drop of roughly ₹5,000 per 10 grams in Indian gold futures, offering a potential entry point for jewelers stocking up ahead of the October-November wedding season.

For NRI investors holding gold ETFs or physical gold, the divergence between gold’s short-term weakness and its long-term bull case creates a strategic question. If Citi’s scenario plays out — a further decline followed by a surge past $6,000 — patient buyers could be well rewarded.

The next major catalyst is the Fed’s end-of-July meeting. A hawkish tone could push gold lower in the near term, while any dovish surprise would likely trigger a sharp rebound.
